speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women published an important document, under the title: Battered But Not Beaten, an investigation of wife battering in Canada.
In this document, a sequel to the book on battered women published in 1980, we find women of all classes and all ages. In 1985, the majority of women in transition houses were young mothers. Fourteen per cent were under 20. Fifty per cent were between 21 and 34. More teenagers and pregnant women who have been battered by their partners are coming to these transition houses.
Many of these women are poor: 43 per cent were living on an annual income of less than $10,000, while 32 per cent had a family income of $10,000 to $20,000.
We also find immigrant, native, disabled, teenage and rural women in this group as well as women living on military bases.
Much has been done since 1980 and much remains to be done. A number of recommendations are directed to the Government, such as increasing personnel and funding for shelters for battered women, including special assistance for child care, the need for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister responsible for the Status of Women to heighten the awareness of the Members of this House, and creating special shelters for batterers. The husbands or boyfriends, not the women, should have to leave the family home. And there is special emphasis on the need for research on the cause and dynamics of family violence and on the connection between violence, alcoholism and pregnancy.
In concluding, I want to say that battered women who choose to stay with their families do not do so out of weakness. In fact, the opposite is true, and this document praises their courage, saying that it takes extraordinary strength of character to stay in that kind of situation.

subsubtopic: UPGRADING OF YELLOWHEAD HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have risen many times in this House to talk about the Yellowhead Highway which runs through Saskatchewan from Manitoba to British Columbia. It is considered, by those of us who live along it, to be the northern Trans-Canada route when travelling across the country. I have pressed many times for federal recognition of this highway and federal funding.
I was delighted when the Government of Canada agreed to a cost-shared $100 million upgrading of the Yellowhead Highway. I was particularly pleased when, just recently, we concluded the Canada-Saskatchewan-Yellowhead agreement involving $22 million of the $100 million to be spent in my home province. Some $15 million of that $22 million will be spent in the general area of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake. It will involve, for example, widening and enlarging the underpass near Borden. There is also a commitment to twin the Yellowhead between Saskatoon and The Battlefords and the first leg will begin shortly.
The Canada-Saskatchewan-Yellowhead agreement is very real evidence of co-operative federalism as the Government of Canada and the Government of Saskatchewan have committed themselves to working together. I would like to thank our Government and particularly the Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament who helped me to make this a reality.

subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF STAFF IN SASKATOON AND MELVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my deepest concern over the reduction of 55 employee positions in Saskatoon and another 47 positions in Melville by Canadian National.
I clearly understand the need for an efficient rail service capable of remaining competitive with other forms of transport. I also recognize the effects automation and modernization will have on the CN workforce. However, 1 cannot overlook the far-reaching effects this shuffle of 102 CN employees will have on these two Saskatchewan communities.
Some of these employees will opt for early retirement. However, most will have little choice but to relocate to Winnipeg where CN is centralizing its workforce. Saskatchewan generated $459 million in major commodities for CN last year. In fact 16 million tonnes, or 18 per cent of all goods carried on CN in Canada in 1986, originated in the Province of Saskatchewan. In light of these figures you would think CN, as a good corporate citizen, would take into account the effects these actions will have on one of its major revenue contributors.
I intend to organize a meeting of senior officials from CN and representatives from the federal, provincial and municipal Governments in order that an amiable solution can be reached reflecting the interests of these two communities and CN's commitment to serve Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: MINERS' MEMORIAL DAY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1937 George Orwell vividly described the life of a coal-miner in these words: "In the western world the coalminer is second in importance only to the man who ploughs the soil". He went on to say that most of the things one imagines in hell are there; heat, noise, confusion, darkness, foul air and, above all, unbearably cramped space.
Tomorrow, June 11, 1987, is Miners' Memorial Day in Cape Breton. We are reminded of the important role coal-mining has played in the history of Cape Breton. Although many mining methods have changed since Orwell's time, the unique character of the miner, the courage and strength that Orwell so well described, have not.
The devastating fire at No. 26 Colliery in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, brings home once again just how dangerous a profession coal-mining is and how the people of Cape Breton have continually had to struggle against adversity. As we turn back the pages of history we remember the tragic loss of 69 men in 1917 in the methane gas explosion which took place in the Lingan mine, and the explosion in 1979 in Glace Bay. We especially remember the origins of Miners' Memorial Day which arose from a six-year series of protests culminating in the strike of 1925 and the death of William Davis.
We can be proud of the coal-mining tradition of Cape Breton and at this time we remember the contributions of all miners and all their families and, above all, we honour those who lost their lives in those tragic accidents.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF BALTIC AND UKRAINIAN NATIONS' SUFFERINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening the fifteenth Ecumenical Memorial Service to commemorate the genocides and continued sufferings of the Baltic and Ukrainian nations will be held at the Notre Dame Basilica in Ottawa, followed by a candle-light vigil at the National War Memorial. Similar ceremonies will be held throughout Canada this weekend.
Ukrainians, Estonians, Latvians, and Lithuanians, together with other captive east European nations, gather each year to commemorate the Baltic Holocaust and the millions of Ukrainians who fell victim to Soviet oppression. The service provides an opportunity to reflect upon the continued persecution and suppression of freedom, national cultures, religions and languages by the Soviet regime.
I urge all my colleagues in this House to join eastern European communities this evening and, by our presence,
June 10, 1987

demonstrate our commitment to the universal principles of freedom, liberty and justice.

subsubtopic: ACCESS TO CONFIDENTIAL TAX INFORMATION-ABSENCE OF SECURITY SCREENING FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday details of a secret government report which investigated the theft of confidential tax information on 16 million Canadians were made public in The Globe and Mail. This damning report is a sorry tale of sloppy and lax security, of unsupervised access to offices containing confidential tax information. Incredibly there was an absence of security screening of any type for employees having access to personal tax information.
The bad news does not end there. The report also concluded that officials in the Minister's Department should have foreseen these serious security problems at Revenue Canada long before the theft of the tax information.
In light of this telling and depressing report the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) should now admit that his Department was negligent in protecting sensitive tax information that millions of Canadians entrusted to the Government. It must never happen again.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF BATTERED WIVES-PUBLICATION OF BOOK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, along with other Members of the House, I was present today when an important book was launched in Canada. Battered But Not Beaten by Linda MacLeod is about preventing wife battering in Canada. It is about the battered and the batterer. It is about the children who also suffer. It is about the shelters and the people who work in them, about the community and our response to a very serious problem.
But the book is also about hope, about love, about support for those who are directly involved.
It is about the progress we have made and the distance yet to go before we can fully understand, control, and ultimately prevent this vicious and particularly hurtful form of violence.
This book is a low-key, serious, sensitive, and enlightening exposition of a complex social problem.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE EFFECTS OF ACCIDENTS ON BOARD NUCLEAR-POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians are asking do we really need nuclear submarines? Are they desirable from an environmental viewpoint? Would Canadians living near coastal waters be safe in the event of an accident? In recent years radiation accidents are reported to have taken place aboard nuclear-powered vessels, including a meltdown.
Experts say that accidents at sea or under the Arctic ice may damage a reactor core and release radioactivity. Although the probability of such accidents is low, it takes only a small release of radioactivity to cause widespread damage.
As reported in a national newspaper, it is the opinion of civilian emergency planners, environmental scientists, and veterans of the United States nuclear navy that the Canadian Government's plans to build nuclear-powered submarines may pose serious dangers to the environment.
The message is loud and clear. Canadians don't want nuclear submarines. The Cabinet should shelve this $5 billion idea of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty).

subsubtopic: HAZARDS POSED BY HIGH WATER LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising in the House today to thank the Government of Canada and especially the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) for their interest and efforts to find possible solutions to the high water levels in the Great Lakes. These abnormally high levels have been plaguing my constituency for a number of years. The people of Sarnia-Lambton thank the Minister for his action plan to assist in the reduction of lake levels.
The Government has recognized the essential role played by the Great Lakes. Lake Huron and the St. Clair River in my constituency are both well-known tourist areas. As well as this, they provide an avenue for commercial shipping, both Canadian and international. They separate Canada and the United States, yet in many ways bring us closer together as we share a common waterway. It is essential that we continue to protect these great bodies of water from environmental problems and shoreline erosion.
The Canadian Government recognizes their importance and appreciates the Great Lakes. By working with our American neighbours we can maintain and preserve the essential characteristics of this great waterway.
I call upon the Government of Canada to continue to respect and appreciate the Great Lakes. For the millions of Americans and Canadians who live on the Great Lakes, I urge the
June 10, 1987

Government to continue its efforts to preserve and protect our homes and jobs on the Great Lakes.

subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND CAPELIN FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Newfoundland fishermen after having spent thousands of dollars getting ready for the capelin fishery now see that the price being offered and the volume demanded by the chief buyers, the Japanese, are not sufficient to maintain that fishery as an economic fishery and they see their families robbed of important income for the coming year.
Is the Minister prepared now to take responsibility to ensure that Newfoundland fishermen will get an adequate and fair price for the capelin?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND CAPELIN FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not the intention of the Government of Canada that the fishery of Newfoundland be nationalized as might be the direction which the Hon. Member would advocate.
We are expecting a very successful inshore fishery in Newfoundland this year partly as a result of the corrective measures I took last autumn at the urging of the Newfoundland Inshore Fisheries Association. We cannot determine prices, or subsidize prices directly, for reasons the Hon. Member should appreciate. However, we are definitely looking forward to this year as a very good year for the fishermen of Newfoundland and Fabrador.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MARKETING AGENCY BE ESTABLISHED

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary to nationalize the Fisheries in order to have a decent pricing strategy in place. This problem happened last year. It is happening this year, and it will go on happening unless the Government takes action. The Minister should be aware of the need and desire for a proper marketing strategy and marketing agency for capelin. Is he prepared now to have a marketing agency for the capelin? And is he prepared to use some of the funds promised to the Atlantic area through the Atlantic Opportunities Agency to ensure that agency is able to function and get a fair price for Newfoundland fishermen?

subsubtopic: REPORT ON BATTERED WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and concerns a very distressing report on battered women in Canada which was released today. I wonder if the Minister will tell us if he will respond favourably to the prime recommendation of this report which is for federal initiatives for funding so that we can end this problem by reducing it gradually, and so that transition houses and shelters can work toward education and prevention so there will no longer be one million battered wives in Canada.
June 10, 1987

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: REPORT ON BATTERED WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report from the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women is an extremely important one. As was mentioned, for example, by the Hon. Member for Guelph in his statement to the House today, the report on which I had a briefing earlier from Ms. Gold lays out very clearly the wide-ranging complexities of the issue. I also think the report indicates that there has been some progress made but we have a long way to go yet.
I might say to the Hon. Member and to the House that this matter was placed on the agenda of the Minister responsible for federal-provincial social affairs in January. I intend to take the issue back and make further recommendations to my cabinet colleagues along with my colleagues who have similar responsibilities in this field.

Mr. Speaker, for every one woman who enters a shelter for battered wives, another is turned away because of lack of funds. We still have a very long way to go.
I wonder if the Minister would be more positive in his response and would really deal with the fundamental recommendation that there must be federal initiatives so that there will be not just emergency response but a comprehensive approach to education and prevention for dealing with this problem and eliminating the shameful condition of the existence of battered wives.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to minimize at all the recommendations made by the advisory council but I think Hon. Members should also keep in mind that there have been two changes made in the very specific area the Hon. Member has raised in her question. There has been an increase in the number of transition homes. I along with my colleague, the Minister responsible for CMHC, will have to expand that social housing so that there will be an additional number of spaces.
Second, I changed the Canada Assistance Plan regulation for a needs test. I felt that that was not appropriate. If a woman presents herself at a transition home, her needs are not financial, her needs are psychological and social and can be so identified quickly. That provision has been changed so that women can access those homes under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Earlier in my response I said that we will look at the report very carefully. I will come back to the House and my cabinet colleagues for further recommendations and action.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Immigration. Every single NGO in the country is unanimously opposed to the fundamental tenets of this legislation. Given all that, will the Minister begin to promote and defend the constituency he is responsible for in Cabinet by eliminating the pre-screening process and the safe third country concept which have the effect of turning people away even before they reach an oral hearing before a refugee board? subsubtopic: BILL C-55-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Hon. Member for York West is fully aware of the opinion of Canadians concerning the legislative measure we tabled with respect to immigration and the status of refugees.
I would suggest that the Bill will come up for second reading debate in the very near future. I am even more convinced that our propositions reflect the views of most Canadians concerning the measures we must take to let genuine refugees gain access to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister also knows the opinion of Canadians, some 75 per cent of whom want a fair refugee system. He and the Government are misleading Canadians if they continue to say that this system is fair and humane, because it is everything but.

Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to your attention and that of all Hon. Members that there are three Members of this House who entered Parliament for the first time in the general election of June 10, 1957.
The Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), Nova Scotia, is still a tower of strength in our caucus and the House and a strong voice for freedom. He has served with dignity and honour and has made a tremendous contribution to this House, to Nova Scotia, and to Canada.
The Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates), Nova Scotia, has over 30 years served with dedication and commitment, never wavering in his loyalty to his Party and his country, serving in many capacities in the House and indeed in the Party. Of course we must acknowledge in our midst the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), Saskatchewan, who served as a Minister in that first Diefen-baker Government and subsequent Governments. His imagination and creative approaches to dealing with our mutual problems have certainly made a notable contribution to our country.
There are many other outstanding Members from other Parties who came into the House in the 1957 general election. Many have since gone on to other fields of endeavour. 1 would like to take this opportunity, on behalf of my colleagues, to congratulate and thank them all for their outstanding service and their distinguished contribution to this House and to Canada.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext:
At that time, the three Members mentioned by the Deputy Prime Minister were also elected to this House of Commons; the Members for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) and Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates), both from Nova Scotia, and, of course, the Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) from the Province of Saskatchewan.
I want to say to all three hon. gentlemen that no greater tribute can be paid in this country than to enjoy the confidence of one's fellow citizens, for whatever length of time, but 30 years is a hallmark of which each of them individually ought to be proud. It is a tribute to the sacrifices they and their families have made. I want to congratulate all three of them most heartily.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext:
I, too, in breach of the rules, would like to recognize Michael Starr whom I knew as Minister of Labour and for whom I retained a very warm friendship. He enjoyed the respect of Members from all sides of the House when he was in this place.
Since the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain is here in the House this afternoon I want to say to him that in my view he has never been given the credit he deserves for having authored the northern vision. Mr. Diefenbaker made that a popular concept in Canada. He opened up our lands north of the 60th parallel to Canadian attention. The Roads to Resources program was his. The farmers of this country will always remember him as a spectacularly successful Minister of Agriculture.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON

In any event, to all three gentlemen, congratulations, a generous thank-you from your fellow citizens, and wishes of good health, good future. We are proud to have known you.

Crouse), Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates), and Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). We take great pleasure today in recognizing their contributions to the House of Commons and Canada for so many years. We appreciate the fact that through their efforts Canada is a better place today.
The fact that the three Members being honoured today have served this House for 30 years tells us a great deal about what their constituents think of them having given them the ultimate vote of confidence for so many years. The fact that these individuals have been in this House serving the people of Canada in this capacity for 30 years also tells us a great deal about their perseverance and their commitment to the principles of democracy and parliamentary procedure.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank all Hon. Members for mentioning the names of the three of us who are in the House today and that of Mike Starr. I would like to say something a little different from what would ordinarily be expected on this occasion.
I recall when a Member from one of the York ridings had been in the House for 30 years and the Prime Minister had made him an honorary Privy Councillor. The House began to scream "Speech, Bob, speech". He had never made a speech in 30 years. He rose in his place and made the shortest speech I think this House has ever heard. He said, "If you guys would speak a lot less you would last a lot longer", and he sat down.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext:
In the history of the British Parliament there was one Member who made one speech in the House which was so well received that he never spoke again for 40 years. When he went to Ireland to become a Member of Parliament in the new Irish House they asked him why he had kept quiet for so long. He was a very able person. He said, "When you do something you cannot do better at, take it as granted and do not try to do any better". His name was Hamilton too, but that is beside the point.
Some of you may have noticed that in the last few years 1 have not spoken as much as 1 used to. I have learned from fellows like Bob McGregor and the Irish Hamilton of 150 years ago.
I would like to make one serious remark. On June 10, 1957, Canada was living perilously close to a one-Party type of government. I do not mean that in any harsh sense at all. The
Members of Parliament
mere fact that the Conservative Party came back to power, with a minority Government admittedly, was the first break in this tendency.
In addition, never in the history of Parliament had there been so many veterans in the House. Those of us who had survived the war came in here in large numbers in the elections of 1957 and 1958. We brought back to this House an attitude which I think deserves some consideration at this particular moment.
We were well convinced that our efforts abroad would have to be repeated unless we learned to work together, not only within our nation but with other nations as well. I am doubly glad to see my friend, Mike Starr, in the Gallery because we set out to try to co-operate with the provinces.
I well remember in 1958 when we were hard pressed to provide jobs for people. We had a high unemployment rate in those days of about 6 per cent and were catching Hail Columbia from the Opposition. Bill Hamilton, the Postmaster General, and I were doing our level best to build post offices across the country and clear up the bush. We were spending a lot of money but not creating many jobs. Mike Starr suggested that we go to the municipal Governments which had lots of jobs they wanted done but no money.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext:
As the House very well knows, municipalities are the creatures of the provinces. But how did Mike Starr get around that? He simply proposed to the municipalities that all of these programs were eligible for help if they could get the consent of the provincial Government. One had to see the reactions of the provincial Governments. How can one turn down a request from a municipality to have something done in its riding when nothing has to be spent?
I can still remember Premier Duplessis of Quebec calling me and saying: "That Mike Starr, he is a devil. He puts a proposal before me that I cannot refuse". He thought the world of Mike, who was a very sensible person. He only dealt with Duplessis over the phone.

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF MR. CROUSE, MR. COATES, AND MR. HAMILTON
speechtext:
Let me also say that, to my recollection, Mike Starr was the first person to describe the type of program we were conducting with all the provinces and territories as a co-operative type of government. I changed that name somewhat, to co-operative federalism.
I was pleased that the succeeding administration of the Right Hon. Mr. Pearson accepted this doctrine. However, that administration made a slight mistake. It called all the provinces together to deal with them as a group. Confrontational politics could never work in that sort of situation. They must be dealt with individually and let each province have a different arrangement.

June 10, 1987
Unemployment Insurance
Today, I not only want to give credit to the Government of the day but to point out that we had a group of people in the caucus who were very conscious of the fact that the only way to keep peace in the world was to co-operate not only with our own institutions in the country, but to co-operate on an economic basis with all other countries in the world. We are one world economically, we are one country nationally, and the only way we can make it work is through co-operation. All that this Government has done is simply to put it in a written form. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, this is an amendment to the Criminal Code to permit the prosecution within Canada of war criminals found here. The Bill comes from a recommendation of the Deschenes Commission to the same effect. This recommendation has been agreed to by the Government. Although the report was received as long ago as last December by the Government no action has been taken. subsubtopic: CALL FOR INQUIRY INTO USE OF CHEMICAL PESTICIDES
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, it is my pleasure, and indeed, an honour to present petitions on behalf of the residents of Kamloops, Monte Lake, Copper Creek, Argenta, Kaslo, New Denver, Nakusp, Vancouver, North Vancouver, Burnaby, Delta, Lillooet, Bridge Lake, Williams Lake, 100 Mile House, Salmon Arm, Ladner, Surrey and other places.
The petitioners are concerned about the increasing number of chemicals used as herbicides and insecticides which they believe have been proven to have harmful effects on human health. They believe that these chemicals also produce short and long-term harmful effects on non-target organisms, soil and water. They are, therefore, asking the House of Commons to initiate a full public inquiry into the safety, testing, registration and regulation of the use of pesticides and the examination of alternative ways of controlling pests, such as biological control and plant-derived pesticides.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise with a petition which indicates that troubles in many parts of the world are causing people to seek safety from persecution by coming to Canada.
Canada has established standards of refugee status determination but our existing procedures have broken down under unexpected strains. The standing committee of Parliament has proposed a new procedure for refugee determination which is quicker and fairer than the one now in force. This proposal has support among all Parties in Parliament as well as the Canadian Council of Churches, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress and other groups and individuals.
Procedures recently adopted that turn away refugee status claimants from ports of entry before their claims are examined put real refugees at risk. Therefore, we, the undersigned petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that the Government and Parliament enact legislation that will

embody the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of refugee claimants before a refuge board, independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings for every claimant in Canada and an adequate opportunity to arrive in Canada to make this claim.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a petition from a number of Canadians concerned that conditions in many parts of the world are causing people to seek safety from persecution by coming to Canada. They point out that in the past we have had standards for refugee status determination but that these have broken down under unexpected strain. They also point out that the standing committee of Parliament has established a new procedure which has the support of all Parties and of many other groups in Canada concerned with refugees, but that the present procedures which have been adopted turn away refugee status claimants from ports of entry before their claims are examined, which puts real refugees at risk.
Therefore, the petitioners call upon Parliament to ensure that the Government and Parliament enact legislation which will embody the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of refugee claimants before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings for every claimant in Canada, and adequate opportunity to arrive in Canada to make this claim.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CHANGES TO UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a petition from a number of residents of Toronto who are concerned about the subject of unemployment insurance and point out the large amount of money spent in income transfers in other provinces and the necessary consideration of these things by the Forget Commission, but the unfortunate recommendations made by the commission which would force 62 per cent of the unemployed to live on less than $140 a week.
Therefore, the undersigned, your petitioners, call upon Parliament to reject any legislation designed to eliminate federal contributions to the unemployment insurance program and to reduce unemployment benefits for unemployed Canadians.

subsubtopic: LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS AT ARMED FORCES BASE AT GOOSE BAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I also have a petition from a number of people, about a hundred people, living in Toronto who are concerned about the low level flight training of pilots in NATO at the Canadian Forces Base in Goose Bay, Labrador.
Apart from the damage to the local native life, they point out that this training program is a provocative and aggressive war-fighting action that tends to endanger world peace.
Therefore, your petitioners call upon Parliament to ensure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will end all low level flight training at the Goose Bay Canadian Forces Base and cease negotiations with NATO for the establishment of a larger base there.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, finally I have a number of petitions, about a hundred petitions, from residents of Toronto who are concerned about immigration, particularly about the refugee program of the Government.
They point out that whereas the previous system broke down under strains, it is necessary to adopt the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, which has support from the Council of Churches, the Bar Association, the Jewish Congress, members of all Parties, and other groups and individuals, and which would particularly embody the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of refugee claimants before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to these hearings for every claimant in Canada, and adequate opportunity to arrive in Canada to make this claim.
As in duty bound, your petitioners will ever pray.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO RESTORATION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the pleasure of introducing a petition signed by numerous constituents living mainly in the City of Regina.
They petition Parliament to defeat the motion introduced on February 16 supporting the principle of the restoration of the death penalty in Canada.
The petitioners point out that to kill people who kill people to show that killing people is wrong is morally indefensible. They share the belief that returning evil for evil contributes to the disintegration of the moral integrity and social well-being of the society in which it is introduced.
They also point out that as a member in good standing of the United Nations, Canada should be supporting the United Nations in its efforts to eradicate the death penalty in all nations of the world, rather than undermining Canada's reputation as a leader among civilized nations.
Therefore, it gives me great pleasure to present the petition to the House.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29 FRENCH GOVERNMENT'S ISSUANCE OF PERMITS TO DRILL FOR OIL AND GAS IN CANADIAN WATERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me today to ask leave, pursuant to Standing Order 29, to propose a motion to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the issuance by the Government of France of drilling and exploration permits to foreign and French companies to drill in Canadian sovereign waters.
I make this request in the interest of ensuring that Canadians, and more important Newfoundlanders, have an opportunity to air fully in the House all the consequences and implications of such extraordinary action which has been taken in recent days by the Government of France.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I think my hon. friend is making a serious error in fact, which 1 should like to point out to the Chair.
June 10, 1987

In fact the Government of France has not issued drilling permits. Neither has the Canadian Government issued drilling permits.
The permits which were issued were exploration permits, issued by the Government of France and by the Government of Canada, into disputed areas. Both Governments have issued permits to-
